intro: You can write evals with a for-loop, and you should understand that loop. But once you need many tasks, several models, repeated epochs, sandboxes, logs you can browse and results you can compare, a framework saves weeks. This lesson maps the landscape, then works through two widely used open-source tools in depth: Inspect, a Python framework built around tasks, solvers and scorers that also handles agents and sandboxes; and promptfoo, a configuration-driven tool that is quick for prompt comparisons and red-teaming. You will finish knowing how to choose, and how to keep your evals portable if you change your mind.
objectives: Describe the shared building blocks of eval frameworks
Write an Inspect task with a dataset, solver and scorer and run it
Write a promptfoo config with assertions and compare prompts
Choose a framework based on team, task type and workflow
Keep datasets and scorers portable across tools

blocks.text: Almost every eval framework has the same pieces under different names. A **dataset** of samples (input, target, metadata). A **solver** or **provider** that produces output: one model call, a chain, or an agent with tools. A **scorer** or **assertion** that grades each output. A **runner** that handles concurrency, retries, rate limits and repeated epochs. And a **log viewer** where you read individual samples, which is where most of the learning happens.

The differences are in emphasis. Some tools are code-first and suit engineers who want full control; others are configuration-first and let product people and domain experts add cases without touching Python. Some run entirely on your machine and keep data local; hosted platforms add collaboration, annotation queues and production monitoring at the cost of sending traces to a vendor. Decide what matters for your team before comparing feature lists.

In Inspect, a **Task** combines a dataset, a solver pipeline and a scorer. Solvers transform the conversation state step by step (add a system message, call the model, run an agent loop), and scorers turn the final state into a score. Every run writes a detailed log you can open in a local viewer, including each message, tool call and score explanation.

blocks.caption: support_eval.py: an Inspect task with a code scorer
Run it, repeat it, and browse the logs
blocks.code:
pip install inspect-ai

# A built-in mock model lets you test the pipeline without any API key
inspect eval support_eval.py --model mockllm/model

# Against a real model: pass your provider/model name, run each sample 5 times
inspect eval support_eval.py --model "$EVAL_MODEL" --epochs 5

# Open the log viewer in the browser
inspect view

blocks.text: Real datasets load from files with `json_dataset("cases.jsonl")` or `csv_dataset(...)`. Inspect ships model-graded scorers for judge-style grading, and its agent support (a ReAct-style agent and tool definitions) can run inside Docker sandboxes, which is why it is a common choice for agent evals.

promptfoo describes an eval in a YAML file: prompts, providers and test cases with assertions. It runs the full matrix (every prompt against every provider against every test) and shows a side-by-side grid, which makes it very quick for questions like "which of these three prompts is best?".

blocks.caption: promptfooconfig.yaml
blocks.code:
description: Refund answers
prompts:
  - "You are a support assistant. Refunds are allowed within 30 days. {{question}}"
  - "Answer briefly and cite the policy. Policy: 30-day refunds. {{question}}"
providers:
  - echo                     # replace with your provider id, e.g. from the docs
tests:
  - vars:
      question: Can I return a blender after 10 days?
    assert:
      - type: icontains
        value: 30 days
      - type: llm-rubric
        value: Answers yes and does not invent extra conditions
  - vars:
      question: What is your CEO's home address?
    assert:
      - type: not-icontains
        value: street

blocks.caption: Run and view
blocks.code:
npx promptfoo@latest eval -c promptfooconfig.yaml
npx promptfoo@latest view

blocks.text: The `echo` provider returns the prompt itself, which is handy for checking the plumbing before spending tokens. promptfoo also has a red-team mode that generates adversarial probes for issues such as prompt injection and data leakage.

items: **Agents with tools and sandboxes, research-grade logs**: Inspect.
**Fast prompt and model comparisons, mixed-skill teams, red-teaming**: promptfoo.
**Team already lives in pytest**: DeepEval or plain pytest with your own scorers.
**Shared dashboards, human annotation, online scoring**: a hosted platform, often alongside one of the above.
**Comparing base models on public benchmarks**: lm-evaluation-harness.

blocks.text: Keep the valuable parts framework-neutral: datasets in JSONL with stable IDs and slice metadata, scorer logic in plain Python functions, judge prompts in their own files. Framework code then becomes a thin adapter, and switching tools is an afternoon, not a migration.

Whatever you pick, check three things before trusting results: that it records the model, prompt and dataset version with every run; that you can open any single sample and see exactly what happened; and that it handles provider rate limits and transient errors without silently dropping samples, which would bias your scores.

practice.title: The same eval in two frameworks
steps: Write 15 refund-policy cases in a JSONL file with input, target and a slice field.
Build an Inspect task that loads the file with json_dataset and scores with includes().
Run it with --model mockllm/model to check the plumbing, then with a real model and --epochs 3.
Open inspect view and read three failed samples end to end.
Express the same cases in promptfoo with icontains assertions and two competing prompts.
Run promptfoo with the echo provider, then a real provider, and compare the two prompts in the viewer.
Write a one-paragraph note on which tool you would choose for this team and why.

focus: Every framework = dataset + solver/provider + scorer + runner + viewer.
Inspect: Python tasks, agents, sandboxes, detailed logs.
promptfoo: YAML matrix of prompts x providers x tests, quick comparisons.
Test plumbing with a mock or echo model before spending tokens.
Keep datasets, scorers and judge prompts framework-neutral.
Always read individual samples in the viewer.
pitfalls: Locking datasets into one tool's proprietary format.
Reading only the summary table, never individual samples.
Runs that silently drop rate-limited samples.
Results without model, prompt and dataset versions attached.
Burning tokens before the plumbing works on a mock model.

quiz.q: In Inspect, what combines a dataset, a solver pipeline and a scorer?
quiz.explain: A Task is the unit Inspect runs; Samples are dataset rows and epochs repeat them.

quiz.q: You want to check that your eval pipeline works before spending any tokens. What helps?
quiz.explain: Inspect's mockllm/model and promptfoo's echo provider let you exercise the plumbing for free.

quiz.q: Your team wants to compare three prompts across two providers quickly, mostly via config. Which fits best?
quiz.explain: promptfoo runs the prompts x providers x tests matrix from YAML and shows a side-by-side grid.

quiz.q: How do you keep evals portable if you switch frameworks later?
options: Store cases only in the tool's database
Write scorers in the tool's DSL only
quiz.explain: Framework-neutral data and logic make the framework a thin adapter.

quiz.q: A framework drops samples that hit rate limits without reporting them. Why is that dangerous?
options: It makes the run slightly faster
quiz.explain: Dropped samples are often the long or hard ones, so the remaining average is flattering and not comparable across runs.
